results.prompt: Explain how shares, bonds, mutual funds and ETFs differ, especially diversification and liquidity. Give a neutral comparison with sources where available.
results.expected: Expected: **I**. Check support for each requested concept, accurate citations where present, and visible qualification of any permitted model-knowledge section. This asks for education, not personal investment selection.
results.answer:
Model knowledge (not verified against retrieved sources):
Shares represent ownership in a company. A shareholder may benefit if the share price rises and may receive dividends, but neither price gains nor dividends are assured. A bond is a loan to an issuer, which promises interest and repayment of principal under the bond’s terms; payment depends on the issuer’s ability to meet those obligations. A mutual fund pools investors’ money to invest in a portfolio and is typically bought from or redeemed through the fund at a calculated price. An ETF is also a fund, but its units trade on an exchange. These are general descriptions; structures and terms can vary.

Model knowledge (not verified against retrieved sources):
Holding shares or bonds from more than one issuer can spread exposure, while a mutual fund or ETF can hold a range of investments in one fund. The actual diversification depends on what the fund owns: a narrowly focused fund may still be concentrated. Spreading investments can reduce the effect of a setback in one holding, but cannot eliminate all losses or market-wide risk.

Model knowledge (not verified against retrieved sources):
Liquidity is how readily an investment can be converted to cash, and it can vary even within each category. Shares and ETF units may be traded on an exchange during trading hours, but a sale price is not guaranteed and trading costs or the gap between buying and selling prices can matter. ETF trading does not guarantee that its underlying holdings are equally easy to trade. Bonds can differ widely in how actively they trade. Conventional mutual funds are generally transacted through the fund rather than traded on an exchange, and dealing times and redemption terms depend on the fund. Check the relevant product documents for actual trading, settlement, and withdrawal arrangements.

MoneySense defines liquidity as how easily or quickly an investment can be converted to cash, and gives shares versus property as an example: shares can typically be bought and sold more quickly than property. [What is investing?](https://www.moneysense.gov.sg/investments/what-is-investing/)

ETFs are investment funds listed and traded on a stock exchange; investors’ money is pooled and invested according to the ETF’s stated objective. [Guide to ETFs: Understanding Exchange-Traded Funds](https://www.moneysense.gov.sg/guide-to-etfs-understanding-exchange-traded-funds/)

The CPF Board describes mutual funds and ETFs as professionally managed products that provide diversification across a mix of asset classes. [A beginner's guide to investing in Singapore](https://www.cpf.gov.sg/member/infohub/educational-resources/a-beginners-guide-to-investing-in-singapore)

The available source passages do not sufficiently define shares or bonds, compare diversification from individual holdings with fund diversification, or compare liquidity across all four investment types.

results.note: Neutral comparison; retrieved citations and permitted model knowledge are separated with evidence limits.
